newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-CHAMPION KAFELNIKOV SURGES PAST DAMM.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CHAMPION KAFELNIKOV SURGES PAST DAMM.

text.p: Yevgeny Kafelnikov arrived at Roland Garros claiming it would take a miracle for him to retain his French Open title but Monday's opening efforts suggested the Russian will not depart without a fight.

The defending champion showed few signs of rust despite his three-month injury absence from the tour this year as he breezed to a comfortable 6-2 6-4 6-4 win over Martin Damm from the Czech Republic on a warm, sunny Parisian day .

In a wide-open tournament, anyone with a clay court pedigree can consider themselves possible contenders and Kafelnikov's self-doubt seemed to evaporate with every point he won against the perspiring Damm.

"I was looking in a magazine yesterday and saw my chances of winning the title rated as two percent," said Kafelnikov afterwards. "I feel sort of embarrassed. I just want to prove I'm not as bad as everyone thinks."

Only Thomas Muster, champion in 1995, has beaten Kafelnikov on the red clay of Roland Garros in the past two years but the welcome he received from a languid centre court crowd suggested many had read the same article.

"My first impression was that the crowd didn't know I was defending champion," admitted Kafelnikov, sidelined in the build-up to the Australian Open in Melbourne when he broke a finger in his right hand while pounding a punch-bag.

"I felt a lot of pressure but the first round of any tournament when you're defending your title is difficult. Mind you, the first set was so quick I didn't have time to think about being defending champion."

It took the 23-year-old just 27 minutes to take the first set which he clinched with three successive aces and, although the 50th-ranked Damm's resistance increased, there was never any doubt about the result.

"I'm sure the longer I'm in the tournament the better I'll play," said Kafelnikov, who has reached only one semifinal all year. "I feel I can play much much better. I can do everything better, but there's still a fortnight before any miracle happens."
His rivals will take due note, although Kafelnikov himself tipped the serve-and-volley candidates to do better than normal.
"The court is fast and the balls are lighter which means you must have more control.
"It's difficult to say who's favourite between Pete Sampras and Michael Chang, but I'm sure the conditions are an advantage for serve-and-volley players." REUTER
